In general, GRADE users should not rate down for indirectness unless there are compelling reasons to believe that differences between the question (in terms of population, intervention, comparator, or outcomes) and the available evidence are likely to result in meaningful and systematic differences in the observed relative or absolute effects. This is because some degree of discrepancy between the target PICO elements and the available evidence is inevitable, meaning that all bodies of evidence carry some inherent indirectness. The key consideration is whether this indirectness is likely to lead to meaningful, systematic differences in the estimated effects. If so, rating down the certainty of the evidence may be warranted. Such a decision should be supported by evidence or a clear rationale and explicitly reported.
The guiding principle is that certainty should be rated down when studies with greater and lesser degrees of indirectness yield discordant results. Conversely, if the estimated effects across varying levels of indirectness fall within the same range—or consistently remain on the same side of a relevant threshold—then indirectness is unlikely to have a meaningful impact on the pooled estimate. In such cases, GRADE users should not rate down the certainty of the evidence.
Indirectness due to baseline risk is a specific type of population indirectness. It typically arises when there is uncertainty about the true baseline risk in the population of interest. Rather than immediately rating down for indirectness, GRADE users are encouraged to adopt a more analytical approach. This may involve estimating a more representative baseline risk from external sources, such as longitudinal studies (see "ways to mitigate indirectness" below).
Alternatively, users can consider different plausible baseline risks and examine whether the corresponding absolute effect estimates fall into different effect size ranges. If the absolute effects fall into different ranges, it may be appropriate to rate down the certainty of the evidence due to concerns about indirectness. In contrast, if the absolute effects remain within the same range across the plausible baseline risks, rating down for indirectness is generally not warranted.
A more advanced approach involves plotting the risk difference across a range of plausible baseline risks. This visual representation helps identify whether—and at what point—the absolute effect crosses key decision thresholds, offering a more nuanced assessment of indirectness and its potential impact on decision-making.

Schünemann Graphics author: Carlos Cuello Last modified: 14 Aug 2025 Key message The PICO framework is an essential tool for developing clear and targeted questions for systematic reviews and guidelines. This framework is versatile, extending beyond management strategies to the evaluation of tests, prognosis, and exposure questions. Clearly selecting the target population, intervention and comparison of interest enhances evidence identification, synthesis, and analysis, ultimately facilitating the transition from evidence to decisions or recommendations. Review questions: looking for knowledge Questions about managements strategies The PICO framework is a well-accepted way to structure recommendation questions on management strategies. (1) It requires specifying the relevant population, the intervention of interest, the comparator(s), and the main outcomes. In this chapter, we will discuss how to sensibly choose the population, interventions, and comparators. How to select and rate the importance of outcomes will be discussed separately. The initial step that GRADE users typically follow when developing the PICO question is to select the relevant population. This population usually consists of individuals for whom the intervention is a practical and reasonable management strategy. Next, they carefully select and define the intervention of interest, which can include drugs, surgical and interventional procedures, diagnostic strategies, psychological, or educational interventions. One challenge with non-pharmacological interventions is the degree of specificity or description required. For example, “psychological support” for people with depression may be too broad, encompassing a range of clinically heterogeneous interventions that need to be addressed separately. Considering all types and modalities of psychological support in the same analysis can lead to unwanted inconsistency and inapplicability of the findings. Selecting an appropriate comparator is equally important. If a sub-optimal comparator is chosen or used incorrectly (e.g., regarding dosing or frequency of administration), it may result in an overestimation of the benefits of the intervention of interest. The selection of PICO components should ideally involve relevant stakeholders and experienced methodologists. They collaborate in an iterative process to identify and refine the components of the PICO question. Complex questions Sometimes, a new management strategy is considered as an alternative to the standard of care. In such cases, the recommendation question should compare these two options. Other times, the new intervention may serve as an add-on to the standard of care, requiring studies that compare the standard treatment with and without the new addition. Additionally, the new intervention might be part of a complex "package" of interventions, where one component depends on another. These packages can either replace an existing management strategy or be included as an add-on strategy. These examples are just the tip of the iceberg, as many combinations are possible. In order to frame sensible questions, both a deep knowledge of the content area and the methods used to study potential interventions are required, and thus framing the questions is a task that requires involvement of different stake holders and methodologists. Figure 1 – Simple and complex questions Another source of complexity can arise from the existence of multiple alternatives to an intervention. While a multiple intervention comparison framework and a statistical summary via network meta-analysis can help address this issue, it remains crucial to clearly define the population of interest and the interventions to be explored in the network meta-analysis. This clarity aids in interpreting the evidence, assessing its certainty, and making sensible decisions. Questions about tests In order to identify sensible questions about tests or tests strategies, it is important to clearly establish the role or purpose of a test or a test strategy. Tests can have different purposes; for example, they can be to diagnose diseases or conditions; alternatively, they can be used to identify important differences in baseline risk and prognosis of individuals; or they can be used for monitoring the treatment effect of an intervention. Questions about tests can be treated similarly to other management strategies, as the ultimate purpose of a test, regardless of its role in the healthcare process, is to contribute to improve patient outcomes. In this case the same components discussed before can be used to frame the question: a population of interest, the test-based intervention (or strategy), a comparison test intervention (or strategy), and the outcomes of interest. However, very often there is no direct evidence about the effects on relevant outcomes of different test or test strategies. In these cases, GRADE users may use evidence from diagnostic test accuracy studies to make inferences regarding the impact of using a test. These inferences may be done informally or through mathematical models. When the objective is to identify diagnostic test accuracy studies, the PICO framework can still be used, but it needs modifications: the intervention is replaced by the index test, and it is compared with a reference standard. Another particularity with tests is they are almost never used as a single intervention. Most often, tests are used as part of diagnostic pathways or strategies that lead to establish the approximate probability of a certain disease or condition. Also, tests can be combined with therapeutic interventions, and it may be difficult to estimate their contribution to the final health outcome. For example, the American Society of Hematology guideline panel addressed the following question: In a population with an intermediate clinical probability of lower extremity deep venous thrombosis, what is the optimal diagnostic strategy to evaluate them for suspected deep venous thrombosis? (2) Several combinations and sequences of clinical assessment, D-dimer and leg ultrasound are possible. Also, there is no randomized trials assessing any of the strategies. One important aspect is understanding how individuals value the different health states resulting from the intervention of interest (relative value of outcomes). Additionally, it is often important to synthesize evidence related to resource utilization, cost-effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility, and the impact on health equity. Integrating diverse sources of evidence allows decision-makers to gain a comprehensive understanding of the desirable and undesirable consequences of interventions. This complex question is subdivided in different criteria in the GRADE Evidence to Decision Framework to make the decision-making manageable, transparent, and systematic. From a high level, the Evidence to Decision Frameworks assesses: 1. The net health effect of the intervention (in relation to a comparison) and its uncertainty 2. The variability of individuals’ values or relative importance of the outcomes 3. Contextual factors such as resources, impact on health equity, accessibility, and feasibility Following the PICO framework, recommendation questions are typically framed as “in a population Z, should we use intervention X or Y? One key component of recommendation questions are the words “should” and “use”, although the latter can sometime be replaced by similar words (e.g., “offer”). Both reflect that guideline questions are about concrete actions. Practical advice It\'s very important to formulate guideline questions with specific and actionable focus. Take, for example, the question: "In patients with heart failure, should we investigate the precise cause using additional laboratory tests?" This question, while generally understandable, lacks clarity in its specifics. The absence of defined laboratory tests introduces two issues: firstly, it leaves the recommended action open to interpretation by readers, and secondly, it prevents the assessment of the recommendation\'s impact due to its vagueness. Consider another question: "Does Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) lead to cervical cancer?" This question, although relevant for understanding the mechanism of cervical cancer and the potential effectiveness of interventions like HPV vaccination, doesn\'t suggest a direct clinical action. This kind of question are often called "background question" that serves to inform the context of guidelines, rather than being the central focus. Schünemann Graphics author: Carlos Cuello Last modified: 08 Aug 2025 Key message Limitations in the design and execution of RCTs (also called risk of bias of RCTs), is one of the eight GRADE domains. Among these, it is one of the five domains that can lead to rating down the certainty of the evidence. This domain assesses whether flaws in study design or execution could significantly affect our confidence in where the true value of an intervention is relative to predefined thresholds or ranges. The primary method for assessing study limitations involves comparing studies with high and low risk of bias through sensitivity analyses, using statistical or graphical tools. However, there are scenarios where it may be necessary to rate down the certainty of the evidence, even when sensitivity analyses do not show any apparent differences. What are the limitations in the design or execution in randomized trials? As the name suggests, randomization is the defining feature that distinguishes randomized trials from non-randomized studies of interventions (NRSIs). It involves assigning participants to different groups by chance rather than by choice or preference. The primary purpose of randomization is to minimize confounding bias, which occurs when the allocation process results in imbalances in factors—such as age, sex, or disease severity—that may influence outcomes. These are known as confounding factors. A failure in the randomization process is typically considered a very serious concern. However, randomization and allocation concealment only ensure balance in prognostic factors at the start of the trial. To maintain this balance throughout the study, adherence to the protocol, blinding, intention-to-treat analysis, and complete outcome reporting for all randomized participants are essential. Methodological limitations in trial conduct may compromise the validity of results and also warrant serious concern. How to evaluate the limitations in the design or execution in randomized trials Evaluating the limitations in the design or execution of randomized trials can be approached in various ways, such as using specific tools like the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 (1) or conducting a rigorous analysis based on the general principles outlined in this chapter (table 1). Table 1 – Limitations in the design or execution in randomized trials Limitations Explanation Ways trialists can reduce bias Randomization process Random allocation of participants to the different treatment groups creates groups of similar prognostic profiles and thus, similar probability of experiencing the outcomes of interest Computer generated sequence with allocation concealment (e.g., central randomization). Systematic deviations from protocol Deviations from the intended protocol may change the prognostic similarity between groups established by randomization Blinding of participants, investigators, and study personnel Intention-to-treat analysis Missing outcome data If a substantial proportion of outcome data is missing the prognostic balance between groups established by randomization may be compromised Strategies to increase follow-up Analytical strategies to deal with missing outcome data Outcome measurement Bias in the outcome measurement may arise when the adjudicators are aware of the treatment assignment Blinding of participants, investigators, study personnel, outcome adjudicators Selection of the reported result If different ways to report the same outcome are available, investigators may choose to report the measurement that looks more positive for the treatment group they believe to be superior Use of core outcomes set Publishing a detailed protocol Randomization Process Randomization can be achieved using different methods, including simple randomization, block randomization, stratified randomization, and adaptive randomization. Simple randomization involves randomly assigning participants to different treatment groups without any pre-specified criteria. Block randomization involves dividing participants into blocks of a fixed size, and within each block, participants are randomly allocated to different treatment groups to avoid imbalance and achieve control for certain characteristics of the participants. Stratified randomization involves dividing participants into subgroups based on specific criteria (such as age, sex, or disease severity), and then randomly allocating participants to different treatment groups within each subgroup. Adaptive randomization involves adjusting the allocation of participants to different treatment groups based on the trial data and results. Regardless of the method used to randomize, there is always a specific sequence of randomization underlying the process. A random sequence generation is usually achieved in practice by using a computer. However, any method that involves true chance or true random allocation is acceptable. Allocation to an intervention based on specific characteristics of a person, such as personal identification data, e.g. a social insurance number, or date of admission are not entirely random and, thus, they are not acceptable as a sequence generation technique. Moreover, these allocation methods make it virtually impossible to achieve concealment, which further reduces our confidence in achieving the goals of randomization. Allocation concealment refers to the measures taken to ensure that the randomization sequence is not revealed to the individuals involved in enrolling and assigning participants to study groups. If the individuals involved in the study have knowledge of the study group allocation, they may be influenced by this knowledge and introduce bias into the allocation process. Thus, to ensure that randomization achieves its goal (i.e., creating groups of similar prognostic profiles) the sequence of randomization has to be generated by a truly random method and has to be concealed from the investigators deciding about inclusion of participants. Allocation concealment can be achieved through many methods, including centralized randomization or sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes. Centralized randomization typically involves a coordinating center that generates the randomization sequence and communicates the treatment allocation to the study sites after the individual has been enrolled as a study participant. Sealed envelopes involve the use of opaque and sequentially numbered envelopes that contain the treatment allocation and are opened only after the participant is enrolled and their eligibility is confirmed. Given their nature, methods using envelopes are more susceptible to manipulation by investigators and thus are less reliable than central randomization. (2) Practical advice When assessing the risk of bias of randomized trials, GRADE users should examine how the sequence was generated and how it was concealed. As mentioned before, computer-generated sequences and central randomization are the most appropriate methods to ensure a proper randomization process. It is important to consider that even a perfectly conducted randomization process may not be able to prevent imbalances in the baseline characteristics of the groups within a trial. These imbalances are result of chance and do not introduce bias. The imbalances are more likely to be large when the number of randomized individuals is small than when the number of randomized individuals is large. Deviations from the intended protocol Systematic deviations from the intended study protocol may change the prognostic balance that the randomization process establishes and thus may influence the probability that outcomes, without an intervention, would occur in equal proportions in the intervention and comparison groups. Deviation from the intended protocol may occur at multiple stages in trials. For example, complex interventions that are difficult to implement, like health services interventions, rehabilitation, public health, or surgery, may not be applied to all participants of a trial. If the interventions are applied differently in the different groups, it may bias the results. Other interventions, like drug treatments for chronic conditions for example, require adherence to be effective. Thus, systematic differences in how participants adhere to the interventions may introduce bias in this situation. Blinding One way to prevent systematic deviations from the study protocol is to put in place mechanisms to prevent participants, investigators, study personnel or outcome assessors from knowing which treatment group a participant has been assigned to. The domain of deviations from intended protocol considers the blinding of participants, investigators, and study personnel. The blinding of outcome assessors is judged separately in the domain outcome measurement. Importantly, blinding does not completely protect from deviations from the intended study/trial protocol, i.e., they can still occur at random. However, blinding reduces the chance of creating systematic differences between intervention and comparison groups by participants, investigators, or the study personnel. However, GRADE users should consider that the lack of blinding does not necessarily introduce bias when participants or investigators cannot realistically affect the prognosis of participants. For example, the SoFEA study was an open label randomized controlled trial conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of fulvestrant in combination with anastrozole compared to fulvestrant alone in postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive advanced breast cancer. The trial enrolled 723 participants and showed no substantial effect of fulvestrant on overall survival. (3) Here, it is very unlikely that participants or investigators may have affected the prognosis of participant or the measurement of survival: the trial was conducted in women with poor prognosis, which was unmodified by any of the interventions, and the outcome survival was easy to measure and objective. In general, the lack of blinding is more problematic with outcomes that have a subjective component, are reported by participants, or in situations where participants or investigators can influence the probability of the outcomes. Practical advice A frequent misunderstanding is confusing blinding with allocation concealment. Blinding, also known as masking, refers to the process of keeping participants, investigators, and outcome adjudicators unaware of which treatment participants have been assigned to. Allocation concealment, on the other hand, refers to the process of keeping the allocation of the intervention hidden from those responsible for enrolling participants in the trial. Blinding occurs after randomization, once participants have been included, while allocation concealment happens before randomization has been completed. Intention to treat analysis Intention-to-treat analysis is based on the principle that participants of a trial should be analyzed in the groups they were originally assigned to, regardless of whether they actually received or completed the intervention as intended. For example, if participants were allocated to surgery in a trial that compares surgery with a medication, but they did not receive it, their outcomes would still be analyzed as if they had received surgery. This method reduces the potential prognostic imbalances introduced by participants who cross from one group to another Per-protocol or as-treated analysis are based on the exclusion of participant post-randomization or due to missing participant data, and thus the prognostic balance between intervention and comparison groups established by randomization is often not preserved. Therefore, such analyses may introduce bias in the results and are usually not considered appropriate for efficacy outcomes. Missing outcome data As we discussed above, the exclusion of participants after the randomization may introduce bias in the results. Missing outcome data relates to participants in whom it is not known whether the outcome occurred or not. This typically happens because participants withdraw from the study, or they cannot be located. Since participants typically withdraw from trials for a reason related to the condition and/or the interventions being investigated (i.e., not at random), if an important proportion of outcome data is missing, the result of the trial becomes unreliable. Unfortunately, there is no valid rule of thumb to assess what proportion of missing data is acceptable in a particular trial or body of evidence. To assess the impact of missing outcome data and the risk of bias, GRADE users inevitably need to make assumptions about the data that is not available: 1. A common assumption is that data is missing at random. This assumption underlies many imputation methods used in trials, such as multiple imputation or the last observation carried forward. However, these methods may underestimate systematic differences between participants with and without missing data. Consequently, they are generally not recommended for systematic reviews and GRADE assessments. 2. Realistic assumptions about the risk of the outcome in missing participants: This method involves making a priori assumptions about the risk of the outcome in participants with missing data. A sensible approach is to assume that participants with missing outcome data have a higher risk of a negative outcome with the intervention. (4) This increased risk is quantified using an odds ratio, often referred to as the "informative missingness odds ratio" (IMOR). (5) A survey of 100 systematic reviews, including 653 randomized trials, showed that 6% to 22% of meta-analyses changed their effect estimates in relation to a pre-established threshold under different realistic assumptions (IMOR from 1.5 to 5). (6) Important changes in effect estimates are more likely when the proportion of missing data increase or when the outcome is frequent. Practical advice Making assumptions about missing outcome data should not be confused with intention to treat analysis. Intention to treat analysis should be restricted to how one handles participants with available data, and that dealing with missing data should be treated as a separate issue. Outcome measurement Outcome adjudicators in randomized trials decide and record whether the study outcome occurred or not. Nowadays many trials include investigators with the specific task of assessing the outcomes. Bias in the outcome measurement may arise when the adjudicators are aware of the intervention assignment: they may unconsciously or consciously record data in a way that favors the intervention group they believe to be superior. A way to ensure proper outcome measurement is blinding of outcome adjudicators. Many trials include a committee who review and adjudicate the occurrence of the outcomes, independently from the investigator team. Selection of the reported result When different ways to report the same outcome are available in trials, investigators may choose to report the measurement that looks more positive for the intervention group they believe to be superior. This can introduce bias. This situation should not be confused with the appropriate use of more powerful statistical analytical approaches, for example using time-to-event survival data versus mortality at a fixed time-point. Impact of study limitations on the certainty of evidence Limitations in the design or execution is one of five GRADE domains that may decrease certainty in the results of a body of evidence. Depending on the severity of the limitations, certainty can be rated down by one, two, or even three levels, reflecting serious, very serious, or extremely serious concerns, respectively. Sensitivity analysis The best way to evaluate the potential influence of study limitations is to conduct sensitivity analyses comparing trials with high and low risk of bias. The assessment of individual trials can be made using standardized tools, such as the Cochrane ROB 2.0 tool. (1) Sensitivity analyses can be conducted using both statistical and graphical methods. If the effect estimates from low and high risk of bias trials are discordant, the certainty of the evidence should be rated down or, if prespecified in the systematic review protocol, these studies may be excluded based on the higher risk of bias. Statistical methods often involve comparing pooled estimates from studies with low and high risks of bias using goodness-of-fit tests, such as the Chi-Square test. A significant p-value suggests that the differences between low and high risk of bias trials are unlikely to be due to chance. However, because the unit of analysis in systematic reviews is individual trials, these statistical tests are typically underpowered. Additionally, the tests typically rely on the signal-to-noise principle, so they may fail to detect a true difference if the effect estimates\' difference between low and high risk of bias trials is small or if there is important imprecision in the estimates. Sensitivity analysis can also be conducted using a graphical approach with pre-established ranges for the magnitude of the effect. If the effect estimates from studies with low and high risks of bias fall into different ranges of the effect (e.g., moderate vs. small), rating down the certainty of the evidence may be warranted. Conversely, if the effect estimates from low and high risk of bias studies fall within the same range (e.g., both in the trivial range), no rating down is required (see Figure 1). Figure 1 – Concordance of low and high risk of bias trials . At the top, results are discordant: low risk of bias trials suggest a small benefit, while high risk of bias studies indicate a moderate benefit. In contrast, results at the bottom are concordant, with both low and high risk of bias trials suggesting no important effect. It is important to note that although the graphical method is simpler, it has less power to detect differences. This method requires larger discrepancies between the effect estimates of low and high risk of bias studies, as well as precise estimates. However, if the graphical evaluation shows significant differences, goodness-of-fit tests, such as the Chi-Square test, will inevitably yield a significant p-value and therefore may not be necessary. Other situations that may warrant to rate down the certainty of the evidence Given the described limitations, strong suspicions of study limitations may persist even if not detected in the sensitivity analysis. Below are some paradigmatic situations that may warrant rating down the certainty of the evidence due to study limitations. When assessing study limitations of RCTs, GRADE users should bear in mind that the different techniques used in randomized trials to minimize bias, aim to create, and maintain treatment groups of similar prognostic profiles. Therefore, an extremely serious limitation on one domain, may be enough to rate down the certainty of the evidence by 3 levels. Alternative, an accumulation of less serious limitations may have the same effect. 1. When randomization is compromised Randomization is the key hallmark of randomized trials. When randomization and concealment are not conducted properly, in practice the risk of serious confounding is as high as in non-randomized studies of interventions. Therefore, if there are significant concerns about randomization or allocation concealment in a substantial proportion of studies, or in studies that contribute most to the effect estimates (i.e., carry more weight in the meta-analysis), GRADE users should consider rating down the certainty by 1 or 2 levels, depending on the severity of the concern. 2. Unblinded studies, if investigator or outcome adjudicators can realistically affect the prognosis of participants or the measurement of the outcomes Lack of blinding is problematic when there are ways to alter the prognosis of participants. For example, when there are effective interventions that can be used outside the trial protocol (co-interventions). Also, when the measurement of the outcome can be influenced by the knowledge of the allocation, for instance lack of blinding is a more serious issue with subjective outcomes and participants´ reported outcomes. In general, when most studies in a body of evidence are unblinded, or when the studies that contribute the most to the effect estimates (i.e., carry more weight in the meta-analysis) are unblinded, GRADE users should first assess whether the prognosis of participants or the measurement of outcomes could have been influenced by participants, investigators, or outcome adjudicators. If the answer is no, not rating down is probably appropriate. Meta-epidemiological studies show that lack of blinding in participants, healthcare providers, or outcome assessors may have a modest effect in overestimating the results of trials, (7) and in some instances it may not have any effect at all. (8) But if lack of blinding is indeed a concern, and GRADE users judge that it may have affected the prognosis of participants or the measurement of the outcomes, rating down by one level may be appropriate. Although in theory it is possible to rate down by more than 1 level due lack of blinding, meta-epidemiological evidence and practical experience suggest that those situations are exceptional. 3. If there is an important amount of missing outcome data and realistic assumptions change the effect estimate in relation with pre-stablished thresholds When there is an important amount of missing outcome data, sensitivity analysis using realistic assumptions about the participants with missing information may be required. If the effect estimates with and without these assumptions fall into different ranges of the effect (e.g., moderate vs. small), rating down the certainty of the evidence may be warranted. Missing outcome data may be less concerning when the outcome is infrequent. In cases where the baseline risk of the outcome is very low, even extreme assumptions are unlikely to significantly alter the effect estimates. Similarly, missing data may be of less concern when the intervention effect is large, as larger effects are generally less sensitive to the impact of missing data. Study limitations and other GRADE domains Study limitations may introduce inconsistency in a meta-analysis. If this inconsistency is largely or completely explained by study limitations, GRADE users should not rate down twice, as inconsistency refers to unexplained heterogeneity. Additionally, our ability to detect systematic errors in effect estimates is limited by the amount of random error present in a body of evidence. When there is important imprecision, sensitivity analyses are unlikely to detect discrepancies between low and high risk of bias trials, even if they are present. Simple guide to rating limitations in the design or execution in randomized trials Step 1 – Determine the number of thresholds: The first step in the assessing study limitations domain involves determining the number of thresholds that will be used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence: a. Are you interested in knowing if the effect is on side of a particular threshold (e.g., is the effect of the intervention at least a small benefit?): or b. Are you interested in knowing if the effect is on a particular range (e.g., is the effect of the intervention a trivial, small, moderate, or large benefit?). Obtain these thresholds through consensus or empirical evidence and report transparently how they were set. Intermediate step (only for dichotomous outcomes): Calculate the absolute effect estimates, including confidence intervals, from an appropriate baseline risk and the relative effect or the meta-analytic estimate. Step 2 – Determine target of certainty rating: The second step is identifying the target of the certainty rating, which typically corresponds to where the point estimate of the absolute effect lies. Step 3 – Evaluate the evidence: Compare the results of trials with low and high risk of bias using a statistical or graphical approach. Additionally, identify and consider the paradigmatic situations where it may be appropriate to rate down the certainty of evidence due to study limitations. Step 4 – Decide whether rating down is appropriate: If the results from trials with low and high risk of bias are concordant (i.e., fall within the same range), rating down the certainty of the evidence is likely not appropriate. However, if these results are discordant, or if any of the paradigmatic situations discussed are present, consider rating down the certainty by 1, 2, or even 3 levels, depending on the severity of the identified limitations. A single, extremely serious limitation may justify rating down by 3 levels, while an accumulation of less severe limitations could warrant a similar reduction in certainty. ['GRADE Book Imprecision Author(s): M. Hassan Murad, Ignacio Neumann, Jan Brozek, Miranda Langendam, Philipp Dahm, Holger J. Schünemann Graphics author: Carlos Cuello Last modified: 21 Aug 2025 Key message Imprecision is one of the eight GRADE domains, and it is one of the five domains that can lead to rating down of the certainty of the evidence. Confidence intervals around absolute estimates, such as risk differences or mean differences, are the primary tools used to assess imprecision. When these confidence intervals cross predetermined thresholds—ideally established before the analysis—GRADE users should rate down the certainty of the evidence. Additionally, even when large effects seem precise based on their confidence intervals, it is important to evaluate whether the evidence is sufficiently robust. This assessment depends on the total number of participants and events analyzed. If the effect estimates are based in a small number of participants or events, rating down due to imprecision may still be warranted. What is imprecision? Estimates of effects are derived from one or more studies that represent the available body of evidence to answer a specific question. Since studies are samples of a larger target population, these estimates are associated with uncertainty due to sampling error (also called random error). This uncertainty is reflected in a confidence interval around the point estimate of the effect. As the confidence interval widens, the estimate becomes less precise (i.e., less certain). Intuitively, estimates derived from a small body of evidence are more imprecise than estimates derived from a larger body of evidence, although there are other factors that may affect imprecision. For binary outcomes, imprecision decreases (i.e., confidence intervals narrow): a) as the number of events increases; b) the total sample size increases; or c) when the effect size (difference between the groups) become larger. For continuous outcomes, imprecision decreases when the sample size increases, or the variability in individual measurements decreases. How to evaluate imprecision in studies about interventions The concepts of certainty of evidence and imprecision are closely linked to the existence of defined thresholds or ranges for measuring the effects of interventions. Judgments about imprecision are primarily based on the confidence interval and whether it crosses specific thresholds that are ideally designated a priori (1) . These thresholds may be informed by previous empirical research or developed through consensus among relevant stakeholders. (1) Impact of imprecision on the certainty of evidence As the confidence interval of an estimate widens, it may cross important decision thresholds, making GRADE users less certain that the target of the certainty rating represents the truth. (2,3) Consequently, imprecision is one of the five GRADE domains that can decrease the certainty in the results of a body of evidence. Depending on the severity of imprecision, certainty can be rated down by one, two, or even three levels, reflecting serious, very serious, or extremely serious concerns, respectively. (2,3) Judgements based on two thresholds GRADE users may decide to set two thresholds to judge precision, one for benefits and one for harms. These thresholds could be the minimal important difference, similar to the threshold between no or trivial and small effects in Evidence to Decision (EtD) frameworks, or other thresholds of interest. Although using only two thresholds simplifies the assessment and can lead to higher certainty of evidence, it has the drawback of only indicating the presence or absence of a benefit or harm, without estimating the magnitude of the effect which is required for decision-making. (4) If decision-makers require more detailed information about the effect size such as when using the EtDs (i.e., whether the effect is small, moderate, or large), additional thresholds may need to be considered. Imprecision is judged by how many thresholds are crossed by the confidence interval around absolute effect estimates. Figure 1 – Judgments based on two thresholds . The figure displays four pooled estimates and two decision thresholds. See the main text for further details. In Figure 1, the confidence interval for estimate 1 does not exclude the possibility of no important effect or harm, as it crosses the thresholds for both benefit and harm. Similarly, for estimate 2, the confidence interval crosses the small/trivial threshold (MID), indicating that the option of no important effect is not excluded. Both estimates 1 and 2 are imprecise, as GRADE users cannot rule out the possibility that the observed effects are due to chance—either suggesting no important effect (estimate 1 and 2) or a harmful effect (estimate 1). In contrast, estimates 3 and 4 are precise according to the selected thresholds. For estimate 3, all plausible values are above the small/trivial threshold, suggesting a benefit. For estimate 4, all plausible values lie within the small/trivial thresholds for benefit and harm, indicating no important difference or effect. The judgment of imprecision is based on the number of thresholds crossed by the confidence intervals (excluding the null effect). Estimate 1 should be rated down by 2 levels due to very serious imprecision, as it crosses two thresholds. In comparison, estimate 2 should be rated down by 1 level due to serious imprecision, as it crosses only one threshold. Practical advice A common misunderstanding when interpreting statistical significance involves the role of confidence intervals and their relationship to the line of no effect. Many mistakenly assume that if a confidence interval crosses this line, it implies the intervention has no effect. However, this interpretation oversimplifies the meaning of confidence intervals. Confidence intervals reflect the range within which the true effect is likely to lie and represent the uncertainty around the estimate. Importantly, crossing the line of no effect does not conclusively indicate a lack of effect. A more accurate conclusion of no meaningful effect can only be drawn when the entire confidence interval falls within predefined thresholds for trivial effects—both for potential benefits and harms. Judgements based on six thresholds The rating of imprecision is more nuanced when the ranges of the magnitude of effect include multiple thresholds, such as when using the EtD framework. (2) This approach is particularly useful when the decision to use or not use an intervention may be influenced by the size of the effect on a specific outcome. It is also appropriate when balancing the effects of multiple outcomes or considering other consequences, such as cost. (2) For example, a decision about using chemotherapy for lung cancer may differ depending on whether a survival benefit is judged to be large or small, even if both cross the MID (or small effect) threshold. Given that chemotherapy is generally associated with important harms or side effects, decision-makers are more likely to use or recommend the intervention if the effect is large. As before, the judgment of imprecision is based on the number of thresholds crossed by the confidence intervals. (2) Figure 2 – Judgments based on six thresholds . The figure displays four pooled estimates and six decision thresholds. See the main text for further details. In Figure 2, the absolute estimate 1 should not be rated down, as it does not cross any thresholds that define the ranges. In contrast, estimates 2, 3, and 4 should be rated down by one, two, and three levels, respectively, based on the number of thresholds they cross. (2) Practical advice Is the no effect a relevant threshold? In the context of decision-making, the "no effect" line may not be a helpful threshold. This is because decisions depend on more than one outcome, very small effect sizes may not be considered important by patients and stakeholders, and because a null effect is actually impossible to measure (i.e. what is called “null effect” is in reality an infinitesimally small range around the no effect). However, there are certain scenarios, such as the early phases of intervention development, where the potential negative consequences are not yet fully explored or understood. In these initial stages, the primary focus may be on discerning any effect, whether positive or negative, that the intervention might have. Here, the "no effect" line may serve as a temporary threshold. Conceptually, employing the "no effect" line as a threshold operates under the assumption that the thresholds for small/trivial effects or minimal important differences (MIDs) are congruent with the "no effect" line. Additional considerations when rating imprecision The problem of having a large relative effect on a dichotomous outcome and a CI that does not cross thresholds There have been instances of small studies that produced large relative effects on dichotomous outcomes, appearing precise based on their confidence intervals despite involving a very small number of events. However, the results of these studies are fragile, meaning they could change importantly if the outcomes were different in just one or a few participants of the study, and they can still be due to chance. This phenomenon is partly due to how the confidence intervals for odds ratios and relative risks are calculated: they tend to become narrower with larger effects. (5) When GRADE users face the situation of a confidence interval that does not overlap the thresholds of interest (i.e., no reason to rate down for imprecision based on the confidence intervals) and the effect is sufficiently large (e.g., relative risk reduction or an increase over 50%), it is important to check whether the analysis has sufficient power by assessing the review information size. (6) The review information size (RIS) is based on a conventional sample size calculation: it estimates the number of participants required to demonstrate an anticipated large effect. (5,6) Such numbers can be specified in a forest plot over the corresponding thresholds for large, moderate, and small effect. The actual sample size of the review can also be specified on the forest plot. Then, the numbers of levels that need to be rated down by imprecision correspond to the number of thresholds that are crossed by a line between the actual sample size and the estimate of the effect observed. Figure 3 - Large relative effect based on a small number of events Figure 3 presents a hypothetical situation. Estimate A is derived from a meta-analysis of 100 participants on a dichotomous outcome. Based on the selected thresholds, Estimate A corresponds to a large effect. However, given the small number of participants, this effect appears unrealistically large and is likely the result of chance. We can calculate the RIS to test differences between the observed effect and the thresholds: 10,044 for the large-effect threshold, 1,116 for the moderate-effect threshold, and 496 for the small-effect threshold. Plotting the actual number of participants (n = 100) in the figure and comparing it with the observed effect helps in judging imprecision. In this example, the line representing Estimate A crosses three thresholds. Therefore, rating down for imprecision by three levels is appropriate, even though the confidence interval around Estimate A does not cross any threshold. This approach can also be applied to moderate effects, for example by calculating the RIS needed to show a difference between a moderate effect and either the moderate- or small-effect thresholds. However, it is important not to over-penalize a body of evidence. When large effects are plausible and supported by indirect evidence, small sample sizes are often sufficient to provide enough confidence in the effect estimate. Practical advice The RIS is calculated using a conventional sample size method, but it focuses on estimating the sample size needed to demonstrate a difference between an anticipated large effect and predefined thresholds. For instance, if a large effect is observed but there are concerns about random error due to a small number of participants or events, the RIS estimates the necessary sample size to confirm the difference between an anticipated true large effect and the thresholds for large, moderate, and small effects. It’s important to note that the anticipated large effect, on which the RIS calculation is based, should be an assumption made by GRADE users rather than the observed effect. Since the anticipated large effect is close to the large effect threshold, demonstrating this small difference necessitates a large sample size. However, as we move toward moderate and small effect thresholds, the difference between the anticipated large effect and these thresholds increases, reducing the sample size required. The scenario of very low baseline risk When the baseline risk is very small (<5%), a particular situation may occur: the confidence interval of the relative effect may be wide, but the confidence interval of the absolute risk can be narrow and sufficiently precise for decision-making. In this scenario, even if the review information size is not met, it may be appropriate to not rate down by imprecision. The rationale for being more restrained is that when the baseline risk is very small, the absolute estimates of effect used for decision-making are unlikely to change importantly regardless of how much the relative effect changes. (3,5) This is conditional on the studies having sufficient length of follow up and a rigorous approach of identifying new events (i.e., the small number of events is not due to short follow up or lack of reporting). Overlap of the domains of imprecision and inconsistency The confidence interval in random-effects models, which are commonly used in meta-analyses, is calculated from both the across-study variance and the within-study variance. The across-study variance corresponds to the differences between point estimates, while the within-study variance corresponds to the standard error of the studies included. Therefore, when there is important inconsistency (large across-study variance), random-effects models yield a wider confidence interval than fixed-effects models. In other words, in random-effects models, inconsistency produces wider confidence intervals and less precise estimates. GRADE users should be aware of this "double counting" when using random-effects models and should only rate down for both inconsistency and imprecision if they observe important unexplained heterogeneity along with imprecision in both random and fixed-effects models. Simple guide to rating imprecision in studies about interventions Step 1 – Determine the number of thresholds: The first step in assessing imprecision involves determining the number of thresholds that will be used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence: a) Are you interested in knowing if the effect is on side of a particular threshold (e.g., is the effect of the intervention at least a small benefit?); or b) Are you interested in knowing if the effect is on a particular range (e.g., is the effect of the intervention a no or trivial, small, moderate, or large benefit?). Obtain these thresholds through consensus or empirical evidence and report transparently how they were set. Intermediate step (only for dichotomous outcomes): Calculate the absolute effect estimates, including confidence intervals, from an appropriate baseline risk and the relative effect or the meta-analytic estimate. Step 2 – Determine target of certainty rating: The second step is identifying the target of the certainty rating, which typically corresponds to where the point estimate of the absolute effect lies. Step 3 – Evaluate the evidence: Determine how many relevant thresholds the confidence interval crosses. Step 4: – Decide whether rating down is appropriate: Rate down the certainty by 0, 1, 2 or 3 levels according to the number of thresholds crossed. Step 5 – Further Analysis: If the effect is large or moderate and it is based on a small number of events, you may need to use the review information size (RIS) to determine the required sample size for small, moderate, or large effects to assess if further rating down is required. GRADE offers methods, tools and processes to assess the certainty of evidence and support healthcare decision making, particularly developing recommendations, enhancing the transparency in healthcare decision-making. It classifies evidence certainty ofto four categories (very low, low, moderate and high) based on study design, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and dissemination bias. The Summary of Findings (SoF) tables and Evidence Profiles (EP) facilitate evidence synthesis and communication while Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework supports structured decision-making. Widely applied in clinical, public health and health systems guidelines, GRADE continues to evolve, integrating new methods and technologies
Introduction The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach offers a structured framework for assessing the certainty of evidence and supporting healthcare decision-making, especially in the development of recommendations. Its conceptual foundation supports a systematic, explicit and transparent process that defines the role of evidence, its certainty, and contextual factors in formulating recommendations and making decisions. GRADE acknowledges the need for judgments in this process. Rather than eliminating judgments or disagreements, GRADE enhances transparency by making these judgments and related deliberations explicit and structured (Table 1). It also ensures all interest-holders are contributing to those deliberations. Table 1. Merits of GRADE in comparison to other systems 1. Clear separation between certainty of evidence and strength of recommendations 2. Explicit and comprehensive criteria for rating down and rating up the certainty of evidence 3. Explicit consideration of the relative importance of various outcomes to patients and people 4. Structured framework and transparent process of moving from evidence to decisions 5. Explicit advice to make recommendations even when only very low certainty evidence is available 6. Clear and pragmatic interpretation of strong and conditional recommendations 7. Balance between simplicity and methodological soundness and comprehensiveness 8. Allows for adaptation and adoption of decision and recommendations (GRADE Adolopment) 9. Resources to learn about GRADE are widely available and freely accessible 10. Supported by an international network 11. Allows for innovation, refinement and further development 12. Supported by tools, e.g. GRADEpro Certainty of evidence GRADE defines certainty of the evidence as the "certainty that the true value of an estimate falls within a specific range or above or below a decision-making threshold". (1–3) The type of estimate for which certainty is assessed varies depending on the application of GRADE: in intervention questions, it refers to the treatment effects; when estimating patients’ values, it pertains to the relative importance of outcomes; in diagnostic questions, it may reflect the effect of a diagnostic strategy or, more commonly, the diagnostic accuracy measures of a test; in prognostic assessments, it typically represents a measure of association between a predictor and an outcome; and in environmental health and risk assessment, it generally describes the relationship between an exposure and an outcome. GRADE categorizes the certainty of the evidence as high, moderate, low or very low (Table 2). These certainty levels apply to the body of evidence assessed for each key question, rather than individual studies. However, some assessment (e.g. study limitation) are needed for each individual study in order to assess the certainty of the evidence. Central to the assessment of certainty of the evidence are two key concepts: decision thresholds and the target of the certainty rating. Decision thresholds are reference values that guide judgments about both the size of the effect (e.g., trivial, small, moderate, or large) and the associated certainty of evidence. Eventually they would also inform judgments of balance of effects of an alternative option relative to another (e.g., deciding whether benefits outweigh harms), or support commitment to an alternative (e.g., recommending one intervention over another). The target of the certainty rating refers to the specific range of interest (e.g., a moderate benefit) that is being assessed. It generally corresponds to the range or side of a threshold within which the point estimate falls. The certainty assessment is a 4-steps process: 1. Determining the number of thresholds: The first step in the assessment is to determine the number of decision thresholds that will be used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. The thresholds may be established through consensus or empirical evidence and should be reported transparently. 2. Determining target of certainty rating: The second step is identifying the target of the certainty rating, which typically corresponds to the range within which the point estimate lies. 3. Evaluation of the Evidence: In this step, GRADE users systematically assess potential concerns related to GRADE domains, such as study design and execution, including risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and dissemination bias. Dose effects and large effects may increase the certainty of the evidence. 4. Determining whether to Rate Down or Up: Identifying a potential concern in any GRADE domain does not, by itself, justify rating down the certainty of the evidence. Rating down is appropriate only when the concern introduces reasonable doubt that the true effect estimate may fall outside the target of the certainty rating. The same principle applies to rating up: simply recognizing a factor that might strengthen an inference is insufficient to increase certainty. An analysis is required to assess the potential for confounding or spurious results before rating up the certainty of evidence. Moderate certainty There is moderately confidence that that the true value of the estimate of interest is on one side of a threshold of interest or within a certain range. The true value of the estimate may deviate slightly from the target of the certainty rating (i.e. may possibly fall in a different range). Low certainty There is low confidence that that the true value of the estimate of interest is on one side of a threshold of interest or within a certain range. The true value of the estimate may deviate from the target of the certainty rating (i.e. likely fall in a different range). Very-Low certainty. There is very-low confidence that that the true value of the estimate of interest is on one side of a threshold of interest or within a certain range. The true value of the estimate may deviate significantly from target of the certainty rating (i.e. probably fall in a different range). Similar interpretations can be made for a large effect (e.g., the intervention results in a large reduction/increase), for a small effect (e.g., the intervention results in a slight reduction/increase) or for no important effect (the intervention results in no important difference). Certainty of the evidence about the effect of interventions For interventions, the starting point for rating the certainty of evidence is the study design, broadly separated into two types: • Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) • Non-randomized studies about intervention (NRSI) or observational studies (including but not limited to cohort studies, and case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, or case series and case reports). Although randomized controlled trials are the preferred source of evidence for assessing interventions, GRADE users often need to rely on non-randomized studies, particularly when evaluating potential harms, as well as the feasibility, barriers, and facilitators of implementation. Evidence from both RCTs and NRSI can be valuable, with each complementing the other. (4) In GRADE, a body of evidence from RCTs starts with a high-certainty rating, whereas evidence from NRSI typically begins with a low-certainty rating due to the inherent risk of confounding and selection bias associated with the lack of randomization. However, when a rigorous assessment tool, such as ROBINS-I, is used to systematically evaluate these biases, NRSI may start as high-certainty evidence. Nevertheless, such evaluations frequently reveal a moderate or high risk of confounding and selection bias, warranting rating down by two levels of the initial certainty. (5) Figure 2 – The GRADE approach for rating the certainty of interventions. The body of evidence of one or more studies will start as high or low certainty of evidence (CoE) if it is composed of randomized studies (RCTs) or non-randomized studies (NRSI) respectively (A and B). Five criteria can downgrade the CoE (C), and three will upgrade it when judged to be present (D). Based on these judgements a final CoE is obtained for the whole body of evidence for each outcome (E). If, from the outset, the evaluator uses ROBINS-I to assess the risk of bias of NRSI, the initial CoE should start as high (orange interrupted arrow) and then proceed to downgrade and/or upgrade as applicable using all GRADE criteria. Five domains can lower the certainty of the evidence from RCTs and NRSI These initial ratings are followed by detailed ratings across the five domains that can lower the certainty. The ratings are conducted initially at per outcome level. This requires detailed knowledge of the individual studies included in the body of evidence. In theory, each GRADE domain can justify rating down the certainty of evidence by one, two, or three levels. However, the criteria for rating by two or three levels have not been fully operationalized for domains other than imprecision. Limitation in study design and execution This domain evaluates the risk of bias arising from flaws in the design or implementation of individual studies. The primary method for assessing study limitations involves comparing studies with high risk and low of bias through sensitivity analyses, using statistical or graphical tools. However, there are scenarios where it may be necessary to rate down the certainty of the evidence, even when sensitivity analyses do not show any apparent differences. Three situations when this may be the case are: 1. when randomized is compromised (e.g., non-random sequence generation); 2. In unblinded studies, if investigator or outcome adjudicators can realistically affect the prognosis of participants or the measurement of the outcomes; and 3. If there is an important amount of missing outcome data and plausible assumptions change the effect estimate in relation with pre-stablished thresholds. Inconsistency This domain evaluates whether there are systematic differences across the study results included in an evidence synthesis. By definition, if only one study is available, there is no concern about inconsistency. (6) If inconsistency can be explained by a small number of a priori subgroup hypotheses, GRADE users may choose to stratify the evidence on the basis of these factors. However, if the inconsistency remains unexplained, the certainty of the evidence should be rated down. Statistical measures, such as I² and Cochran\'s p-value, provide an initial assessment of inconsistency. However, the final certainty judgment should be based on examining the effects of individual studies and their relationship with pre-established thresholds or ranges. Indirectness This domain covers concerns about applicability, generalizability, external validity, translatability and transferability of research results to a question of interest. GRADE distinguished population, interventions, comparisons and outcome indirectness in studies of interventions. A special type of indirectness (indirect comparison) results when two or more options are not directly compared within studies. The primary method for assessing indirectness involves comparing studies with more and less indirectness using statistical or graphical tools. However, there are scenarios where it may be necessary to rate down the certainty of the evidence, even when subgroup analyses do not show any apparent differences, for example when there are concerns about the baseline risk estimate. Imprecision This domain evaluates the risk of random error within a body of evidence. Confidence intervals around absolute estimates, such as risk differences or mean differences, are the primary tools used to assess imprecision. When these confidence intervals cross predetermined thresholds GRADE users should rate down the certainty of the evidence. (3) Additionally, even when large effects seem precise based on their confidence intervals, it is important to evaluate whether the evidence is sufficiently robust. This assessment depends on the total number of participants and events analyzed. If the effect estimates are based in a small number of participants or events, rating down due to imprecision may still be warranted. Dissemination bias This domain evaluates whether the accessibility of study results is determined by the nature of their findings. Although there are considerable challenges in judging the presence or absence of dissemination bias, the methods used in a systematic review, the characteristics of the body of evidence and certain statistical tools may be useful when judging its influence on the certainty of the evidence. Three domains can increase the certainty of the evidence of NRSI If, and only if, there is no reason for rating down the certainty of a body of evidence from NRSI, then upgrading the certainty of the evidence may be possible, within the following three domains . Large effect When a large effect is observed, the likelihood that this effect is entirely explained by confounding variables is very low. As a result, the inference of an important effect is strengthened, and the certainty of the evidence can be rated up by one or two levels. An important consideration is that when a large effect is observed, the target of the certainty rating will typically be set at a large benefit or harm. However, rating up the certainty does not imply greater confidence that the effect is actually large. Instead, it means that given the observed large effect, the probability that the true effect lies in the trivial or of no important range is very low. Dose-response gradient As with large effect, the presence of a dose-response gradient has long been recognized as supporting the causal nature of an association observed in NRSI. Such a gradient will often increase confidence in the findings of NRSI and thereby increase the certainty of the evidence. If a dose-response gradient is observed at the outcome level, the certainty of the evidence can be rated up by one level. (7) Opposite residual confounding Confounding variables generally tend to overestimate the magnitude of an association, thereby weakening the causal inference between an intervention and its outcome. However, in certain scenarios, plausible confounding may instead lead to an underestimation of the association’s magnitude. For example, patients treated in specialized centers often have a more severe disease compared to those treated in general centers. If better outcomes are observed in specialized centers, this finding is strengthened by the underlying difference in disease severity. Situations where the opposite direction of plausible confounding is at play are rare. However, when there is a strong rationale, GRADE users may consider rating up the certainty of the evidence by one level. Practical Advice When rigorous tools are used to assess the risk of confounding in non-randomized studies, the three domains considered for rating up the certainty of the evidence can also serve as additional indicators that the risk of confounding is moderate or low. In such cases, since the initial certainty is set at high certainty, the presence of any of these three conditions can justify not rating down the certainty or rating down by only one level instead of the default two. Overlap between GRADE domains Concerns or observations about a body of evidence may overlap across multiple domains. For example, in meta-analyses using random-effects model, confidence intervals reflect both within-study variance (imprecision) and across-study variance (inconsistency). Additionally, study limitations can contribute to inconsistency if results differ between studies with high and low risk of bias. Similarly, when a dose-response gradient is observed, focusing only on the extreme values may also suggest a large effect. A key principle in such cases is to avoid rating the certainty of evidence up or down twice for the same underlying issue. Certainty of the evidence about values Decisions in healthcare require not only evidence about the effects of interventions but also knowledge of the relative importance of the outcomes that interventions prevent or cause. This information can be obtained through a variety of means, including qualitative and quantitative primary research of patient values, qualitative evidence synthesis, or directly from patient representatives. Quantitative methods include the use of health utility ratings and can be used to express how important a health outcome is. Utility values can be obtained through direct methods (e.g., standard gamble) or indirect methods (e.g., quality of life questionnaires) and represent the average value individuals assign to a given outcome or health state. These values range from 0 to 1, where 0 reflects the value placed on avoiding death, and 1 represents perfect health. A related measure, the disutility (1 - utility), is often more intuitive. The higher the disutility, the greater the value individuals place on avoiding a particular outcome or health state. The certainty of studies reporting utility values start as high certainty evidence, but the same five domain used to lower the certainty of the evidence from RCTs and NRSI can be applied, although the operationalization is different. (8,9) Certainty of the evidence about the use of tests The best evidence about the benefit of using a diagnostic or screening test comes from RCTs of test and intervention strategies that directly measure the relevant outcomes. Indeed, if a test fails to improve outcomes there is no reason to use it, whatever its accuracy. (10) However, in many situations, direct evidence from intervention studies is lacking and the evidence from diagnostic test accuracy studies needs to be linked to other data to assess the likely effects on outcomes. This is a two-step process. In a first step, test accuracy studies are evaluated in systematic reviews, and where appropriate, combined in meta-analyses. The appropriate study design to measure test accuracy is observational, and the assessment of the certainty of the evidence therefore begins with a rating of high certainty. The evaluation follows the basic GRADE principles and the five domains for rating down certainty. (11,12) In a second step the best estimates of test accuracy are linked to other evidence, for example data on the prevalence of the condition, its natural history or the effectiveness of treatments. For recommendations based on linking different bodies of evidence, the overall certainty of the evidence involves an evaluation of which data are critical for decision-making. The overall rating is then based on the lowest certainty of any part of the evidence considered critical. Certainty of the evidence about prognosis and exposures Just as the GRADE approach is used to assess the effects of interventions, it can also be applied to questions about prognostic factors or exposures. In these cases, non-randomized studies are usually the most appropriate design and, unlike when used for interventions, they start as high-certainty evidence. The same five domains—risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias—are used to assess limitations in the body of evidence and may lead to rating down the certainty. (13) Evidence Profiles and Summary of Findings Tables To enhance communication and presentation of findings, the GRADE Working Group has developed standardized summary tables. The Summary of Findings (SoF) table is available in different formats to accommodate various needs. However, its core elements remain consistent, including outcome specifications, the relative effect of the intervention with its corresponding 95% confidence interval, an estimate of absolute effects, and the certainty of the evidence rating. The Evidence Profile (EP) provides similar information but offers a more detailed assessment of certainty domains. Like the SoF table, different formats are available to suit specific needs. (14,15) Additionally, GRADE has developed specialized SoF tables to present evidence on values, diagnostic test accuracy, prognosis, qualitative evidence and the effects of exposures. Developing recommendations and making decisions The GRADE working group has developed Evidence to Decision (EtD) frameworks in order to help guideline panels to use the available evidence and to develop decisions and recommendations in a structured and transparent way. (16) Guideline panels typically rely on multiple streams of evidence to formulate recommendations. Ideally, this evidence is gathered through systematic reviews, summarized within the Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework, and used to inform decisions and recommendations. At a high level, the default EtD template for interventions synthesizes evidence on the net effect of an intervention, the variability in values, and key contextual factors, including the FACE criteria: Feasibility, Acceptability, Cost, and Equity. More recently, a new version of the EtD framework has been developed to support decision-making based on evidence from multiple comparisons. For decisions involving one or multiple diagnostic tests, a specialized EtD framework is available. It clearly distinguishes between evidence on test accuracy and the potential impact of test use on patient-important outcomes. It is important to emphasize that the EtD framework is flexible and can be adapted to meet the specific needs of different organizations. Criteria deemed unimportant for a particular organization can be omitted, while additional custom criteria may be incorporated. For example, planetary health considerations may be included as an additional criterion when developing recommendations on animal food sources consumption or interventions that are associated with the release of greenhouse gases. Strength of the recommendations The strength of a recommendation reflects the overall balance between the desirable and undesirable consequences of implementing an intervention. GRADE distinguishes between five types of recommendations (Figure 3). Figure 3 – GRADE recommendations When there is high or moderate certainty evidence demonstrating a clear net benefit, a guideline panel may choose to issue a strong recommendation in favor of the intervention. Conversely, if high or moderate certainty evidence indicates a net harm, a strong recommendation against the intervention may be appropriate. However, such clear-cut situations are rare. More often, the net effect of an intervention is very small, variable or uncertain. For example, when the desirable and undesirable effects are closely balanced, the overall impact may be highly sensitive to assumptions about population or individual values. Additionally, when the certainty of the evidence is low or very low, effect estimates become unreliable, generating uncertainty about the net effect. In these scenarios, conditional recommendations are more appropriate. There are a few exceptions to this rule that are explained in one of the chapters. Those making recommendations or decisions should make all effort to provide a recommendation even if the evidence is of very low certainty because users of the recommendation are looking for answers that they will usually not have the time to explore with the same depth as a guideline developer or health technology assessment body. (17) Furthermore, the middle option of offering either alternative deserves special attention. It should be utilized for comparisons of two active alternatives when the choice between options is a sensible one. When the comparator is no active intervention of standard of care, choosing the middle option is not helpful for users of the recommendation. Offering to use an intervention or not is not providing guidance. Thus, users should choose this options when the intervention and comparator are really deemed equivalent. The GRADE Pro Software The GRADE process from creating a SoF table to interactive EtD frameworks and full guidelines is facilitated by the GRADEpro software (www.gradepro.org). GRADEpro is used by Cochrane systematic review authors to produce SoF Tables and by guideline developers to produce and publish recommendations online. GRADEpro can also be used to develop apps on handheld devices. Conclusions GRADE provides an approach to assess the certainty or quality of a body of evidence by outcome and across outcomes. GRADE also provides an approach to moving from evidence to a decision using EtD frameworks. The strength of the GRADE approach rests in the structured framework for the assessment of evidence independent of the actual intervention or question, and the requirement for explicit processes and transparent judgements. GRADE has been applied to a wide range of healthcare interventions, from clinical to public health and health policy questions. The ease of applying the GRADE approach will vary according to the type of evidence being assessed, the circumstances in which GRADE cannot be usefully applied are rare. The GRADE approach has evolved significantly since its inception in the early 2000s. Like any scientific methodology, it will continue to adapt to meet the evolving needs of decision-makers and to integrate emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence.
